items.title: Show HN: Mago, an open source AI video studio, runs locally with Comfy
items.summary: I'm Alvaro, one of the founders of Mago. With my co-founder Alex (creator of Warpfusion, open source video to video), we built an open source AI video studio specialized in long form content and large volumes of video. It's a desktop app that you can run for free on your own GPU, that uses a portable ComfyUI or can be plugged into an existing Comfy setup. It handles both hybrid production (video to video, AI VFX) and full AI (microdramas, AI series for social etc). Back when Alex was working on Warpfusion, we were discussing making an app for "real" production, meaning hours of video, films, series, etc. We started off building a closed source solution, but we're now going back to our roots. In short: there's a billion AI video tools and it seems like everyone wants to make their own, in fact with the progress of LLMs I'm more and more convinced by the idea of personal software. AI series for TikTok and VFX on a feature film have completely different needs. AI video is also quite expensive still, unless you can run it on your own GPU. So not only can you run models for free, if the app is open you can also fork it into whatever you want! Finally, we've been hearing for more than a year that Comfy can be a little too complex, so we thought, well why not try and make open source plug and play? That's the end goal. Limitations: you'll need an Nvidia GPU with 16GB+ of VRAM and 60GB+ of disk space to host the models (Qwen, Minimax H3). License is AGPL. You can also use closed source models with a Mago subscription. Please try it out and let me know what we should add next!

Launch HN: Momentic (YC W24) – Agents that catch bugs by using your app
items.summary: Hey HN, we’re Wei-Wei and Jeff. We’re building Momentic, QA agents that autonomously plan, explore, and bug-bash controls and user flows in your web, iOS, Android, and (soon) desktop apps to catch bugs. Here’s a demo: https://youtu.be/BFsM-Se1Fh8 We’re both software engineers that spent our careers on dev tooling and infra across companies like Robinhood, Retool, WeWork, and Qualtrics. Testing was always a pain in the ass (esp Playwright and Selenium), so we built agents to do it for us. Modern day software has a ton of bugs and the change failure rate is only growing faster as coding agent adoption scales. LLMs are really good at generating code, but reinforce their own assumptions, write a ton of useless tests, and are bad at visual understanding. On DeepSWE v1.1, Sonnet 5.5 hit 66.2% pass rate when banned from writing tests, versus 65.3% when allowed. OSS end-to-end testing frameworks like Playwright, Selenium, or Maestro force you to hardcode implementation details like XPath, text, or aria-* attributes in your tests. Even with agents, these take a nontrivial amount of time and tokens to build and maintain. In 2023, we saw Nat Friedman drive a browser with GPT-3 via natbot. We were inspired to use this technology to automate the most painful and tedious parts of software engineering: testing. We started with using LLMs to generate and maintain Playwright, but quickly realized that those primitives were fundamentally misaligned with the agentic SDLC. We think the future of QA is agents testing themselves, not writing scripts. Mo is a custom agent harness for catching bugs that builds on the past 3 years of Momentic and millions of test traces from complex, real-world applications. Mo is built for recall: it finds the most real bugs, though Codex is a bit more precise at 86% vs 84%. The tradeoff is cost: Mo costs $2.67 per bug vs $0.80 for Codex, less than Claude Code and Devin. - Self-organizing agent graph. Mo builds a directed acyclic graph (DAG) as it explores. Large product areas automatically fork into parallel sub-agents, each with their own browser or device for concurrent execution. - Specialized agents for domain specific tasks. Planner agents reason over screenshots and video while dedicated locator agents inspect page structure to resolve plain-English interaction targets. Others include image analysis, video understanding, audio generation, and more. - Parallel agents coordinate through cooperative resource leases. Agents can announce that they’re “using” or “modifying” overlapping resources or fixtures. Multiple “using” claims can coexist, but only a single “modifying” claim can be active on any particular one. - Scaled infrastructure. Mo ships with a tunnel that lets users expose private sites and local apps to our hosted agents and infra. A single bug bash can spin up 100s of concurrent browsers and devices. We benchmarked Mo against coding agents on 4 popular open-source apps: Gitea (58.8k stars), Metabase, Twenty (YC), and Saleor, with 1,396 human-labeled bugs. Each agent got the same brief, a fresh E2B sandbox, and no access to source code. Codex and Claude Code used hosted Browserbase browsers, while Devin used its built-in browser. For evaluators, we implemented LLM as a judge (GPT-6.1 Sol) with a human reviewer. Results from a time-boxed 60-minute run: - Mo: 269 bugs, 19.3% recall, 84% precision, $2.67 per bug - Codex (GPT-6.1 Sol + Playwright MCP): 86 bugs, 6.2% recall, 86% precision, $0.80 per bug - Claude Code (Opus 5.5 + Playwright MCP): 59 bugs, 4.2% recall, 80% precision, $4.09 per bug - Devin: 27 bugs, 1.9% recall, 84% precision, $3.89 per bug Mo finds more bugs the more time it has. From 30 to 60 minutes, it went from 177 to 269 bugs (+52%), while Codex gained only 16%. Results: https://momentic.ai/qa-bench Write-up: https://momentic.ai/blog/qa-bench Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/momentic/qa-bench Harness: https://github.com/momentic-ai/qa-bench We just shipped PR testing for Vercel and Cloudflare deploy previews and we’re giving every new signup $250 in Mo spend. Paid plans have higher infra capacity and included usage along with options to top up. We’d love for you to try it out and give us feedback. Feel free to comment here, we’ll be around all day!

items.title: Show HN: Open-source, Lightroom Alternative RAW editor made by photographer
items.summary: Hi, I'm the author of CalibRaw, a free, open-source RAW editor developed for Linux, Android, Windows and macOS. There's no subscription, no account and no cloud. I know many have been posted in here, but I just wanted to share CalibRaw too. V1.4.0 was just released and includes many improvements. CalibRaw focues on performance and performance, not UI focused. I'm a photographer, and i built it over the last 3 months because the existing alternatives didn't work for me. The performance was bad, the processing didn't match what I'm used to, or they where just buggy. Darktable is very cool software, but I just wasn't able to work with it. What it does: - Lightroom-style develop panels: light, tone curve, color mixer, color grading, detail, optics and masks - Optional AI masks (subject, sky, depth, ...) that run locally on your device - Advanced masking workflow - Non-destructive: edits live in sidecar files and your originals are never touched - GPU-accelerated, written in Rust with wgpu, not a web app - Android app using the same engine as the desktop app - Effects like glow, fog, relight and more :D A lot of the processing math is ported or adapted from darktable, and I'm very grateful to its developers. I've been using it for the last 3 months constantly improving it. I'd really appreciate feedback on how the workflow feels, and what could be improved. https://github.com/Duecki1/CalibRaw Not affiliated with Adobe. Lightroom is a trademark of Adobe Inc. For many parts of this project LLM's have been used.

items.title: Show HN: Warsaw in voxels – an interactive 3D map of the city centre
items.summary: Explore central Warsaw in voxels - slightly inspired by Minecraft, and MagicaVoxel. You can change the date, time of day and weather, explore the city, or click on a pedestrian to control them (here a bit of inspiration from Dungeon Keeper). Works best on desktop, but I tried to make it usable on mobile too. The initial load can take a while. It's based on several open datasets, including: - OpenStreetMap ( https://www.openstreetmap.org/#map=6/52.02/19.14 ) - buildings, streets, sidewalks, tram tracks, etc - GUGiK / Geoportal ( https://www.geoportal.gov.pl/ ) - LiDAR for building heights and trees, aerial imagery for colours - Warsaw's city tree database ( https://mapa.um.warszawa.pl/ ) - individual tree species, used for seasonal foliage Open-source ( https://github.com/stared/warsaw-vibe-voxel ), so feel invited to (re)use it as you wish!

items.title: Show HN: Devpush – Self-Hosted PaaS for Docker Compose
items.summary: I wanted Vercel-style deploys on my own VPS. That's devpush. I released the first version last year as a Vercel clone for Python apps [1]. It worked, but I couldn't keep up with feature requests, because every new stack needed its own Docker image. I also wanted it to manage multiple servers and be easier to install. So I rewrote it as a much lighter Docker Compose PaaS. You can deploy it on Cloudflare for free and connect as many VPS as you want. Some of the stuff I think is cool: - No SSH access to your servers required. - Works with any Docker Compose setup. - Backups and restores for volumes and databases. - Git-based deploys and rollbacks. - API and MCP. - Free and open source (MIT). The code is at https://github.com/hunvreus/devpush You can also kick the tires, using the free trial of the hosted version: https://app.devpu.sh/ [1]: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45501279

items.title: Show HN: MxRaven – Programmable email infra for nothing in particular
items.summary: Hi HN, I am Kush, a student founder from India building mxRaven ( https://mxraven.com ). We recently made it available for public use, you can read my post about our launch here: https://mxraven.com/blog/launching-mxraven mxRaven is a programmable email delivery platform for not any one particular thing, but rather a flexible glue which can be used to build anything that requires receiving or sending emails in some form, be it agent mailboxes, personal mailboxes, transactional email, marketing campaigns etc. Think of it as a sort of WAF + Application Layer Router but for the SMTP world with ergonomic SDKs for keeping the developers in the driver's seat. For this public demo ( https://sandbox.mxraven.com/ ), I vibecoded a sandbox that (tries) to preview as many mxRaven features as possible publicly without possibility of abuse. You can try to send or receive emails from and to your designated sandbox addresses and play with some basic subset of programmable rules ( https://mxraven.com/docs/concepts/routing-and-actions/introd... ) You can read the details about mxRaven from the docs https://mxraven.com/docs/concepts/start-here/why-mxraven/ and check out our first-party SDKs we have so far: https://github.com/synqronlabs/mxraven-js https://github.com/synqronlabs/mxraven-go https://github.com/synqronlabs/mxraven-py https://github.com/synqronlabs/mxraven-java P.S. Unlike some of our competition we do not use relays like AWS SES. In fact mxRaven was born from the open source raven library ( https://github.com/synqronlabs/raven ) a high performance comprehensive ESMTP toolkit I wrote in Go. We ARE the email relay, and even the core transport and email auth library is first party and open source, something I am very proud of.
